This 67-year-old has an acute change in mental status with fever (38.9°C), tachycardia, leukocytosis, jaundice and RUQ tenderness with biochemical evidence of obstructive liver injury (elevated bilirubin and ALP with mild transaminase elevation). The combination of fever, jaundice and RUQ pain/tenderness is most consistent with acute (ascending) cholangitis. Negative chest x-ray, urinalysis and initial blood cultures make pulmonary or urinary sources less likely. Murphy’s sign is more specific for acute cholecystitis (which would not typically cause conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and marked ALP elevation), and the obstructive pattern of LFTs favors biliary obstruction with secondary infection. The patient’s confusion represents systemic toxicity/delirium from sepsis related to cholangitis (part of Reynolds’ pentad when altered mental status is present). Thus the single most likely diagnosis is acute ascending cholangitis.

Acute ascending cholangitis (acute suppurative cholangitis).
